summary: The note examines how social media shaped voter opinions in the 2023 municipal elections, using anecdotes from candidates, voters and a journalist. It covers grassroots mobilization and digital campaigning, echo chambers and filter bubbles, platform-specific influence on individual voters, and the spread of disinformation that fact-checking struggled to counter. It concludes that candidates who managed their social media presence well often held an advantage, and that this trend is likely to grow.
one_line: Social media shaped voter opinions in 2023 municipal elections through grassroots mobilization, echo chambers and disinformation, favoring candidates who managed their online presence well.
key_facts: Mayoral candidate Jessica Mendoza launched her campaign in Milltown on September 5, 2023, with a digitally native strategy using Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram.
Retired schoolteacher Bob Evans became more politically active than ever through social media, saying "I was sharing posts, engaging in discussions, and really feeling part of the process."
Social media let citizens uplift favored candidates, engage in dialogue, and support grassroots fundraising efforts with surprising efficacy.
College student Maya Jensen found herself in a social media bubble where everyone she followed seemed to support Councilwoman Gonzalez for re-election.
Campaign messaging, hyper-targeted ads, and selective content sharing contributed to echo chambers in October, and 'filter bubbles' raise concerns about the diversity of information reaching voters.
Voters went to the polls on November 2, 2023.
Local entrepreneur Darren Smith said LinkedIn posts and Twitter threads, not television ads or direct mail, influenced his vote.
First-time voter Lila Rodriguez cited Instagram Live sessions hosted by young local council candidates, who discussed affordable housing and climate action, as a key factor in her vote.
Disinformation surged in the weeks before the election, including rumors, falsified endorsements, and manipulated images.
Veteran journalist Robert Ivy said one city council candidate faced a vicious online smear campaign: "It was a full-time job just to address the falsehoods being spread on Facebook."
Fact-checking lagged behind the rapid spread of false narratives.
In 2023, candidates who adeptly managed their social media presence frequently enjoyed an advantage when results came in.
